newsitem.title: USA: U.S. firms' productivity jumps in fourth quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firms' productivity jumps in fourth quarter.

text.p: The productivity of American business grew at the fastest rate in three years at the end of 1996, the government said Tuesday, reinforcing the picture of a healthy economy with little upward pressure on inflation.

The Labour Department said productivity outside of the farm sector rose 2.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, a sharp improvement from the third quarter, when productivity was flat. It was the largest rise since a 2.8 percent productivity gain in the fourth quarter of 1993.
The increase slightly exceeded the 2.1 percent rise predicted by Wall Street economists.

Still, most experts were not surprised by the strength of the number given the strong 4.7 percent rate of growth in Gross Domestic Product, the broadest measure of the nation's economy, in the fourth quarter.
"With GDP growth up so strongly, you would expect to see big gains in productivity," said Joel Naroff, chief bank economist at First Union Corp.
Nevertheless, Naroff and other economists viewed continued gains in productivity, or output per worker per hour, as crucial to ensuring that inflation remained in check.
A pickup in wages amid reports that businesses have encountered some difficulties finding skilled labour have raised concerns about the potential for wage-driven inflation.
The situation has also led to worries that the Federal Reserve, the nation's central bank, might be forced to raise interest rates in a bid to head off inflation.
But Kathryn Kobe, economist at Joel Popkin and Co., said, "Increases in productivity would allow the best of both worlds."
"Workers could enjoy wage increases while more efficiency on the part of businesses would prevent them from having to pass along those increases in the form of price rises," she said.
While the fourth quarter productivity numbers provided reassurance about inflation for now, a key question was whether the trend would continue.

"The fourth quarter numbers were very impressive but it's not typical of what we can expect in the future," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors Corp., noting part of the gain was a "catch-up" from weak productivity growth in the third quarter.

For 1996 as a whole, productivity rose 0.8 percent, the best performance since a 3.2 percent rise in 1992, but still slower than the longer-term trend of annual growth of slightly more than 1 percent.
In the fourth quarter, productivity jumped as output soared 5.9 percent while the total number of hours worked rose 3.7 percent.
Unit labour costs, which make up two-thirds of companies' production costs, rose 1.4 percent in the fourth quarter after growing 3.3 percent the previous quarter.

In a separate report, the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond said manufacturing activity in the bank's five-state region were mixed during January. The monthly survey of business conditions showed improvement in the service sector.
The Richmond Fed's region includes Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, West Virginia and the District of Columbia.
